rows.question: Who was Pete Liegl, why did he sell Forest River to Berkshire, and what was the incentive arrangement?

result.text:
Who was Pete Liegl: Pete Liegl was the founder, manager, and 100% owner of Forest River, an Indiana recreational vehicle (RV) manufacturer.

Who was Pete Liegl: He died in November at age 80 while still working, having contributed billions of dollars to Berkshire shareholders' wealth.

why did he sell Forest River to Berkshire: Pete Liegl sold Forest River because he wanted to keep running the business while ensuring financial security for his family.

what was the incentive arrangement: The incentive arrangement provided Pete Liegl with a base salary of $100,000 per year, an annual bonus of 10% on any earnings above what Forest River was delivering at the time, and an appropriate adjustment to capital if Forest River made significant acquisitions.

citations.title: Berkshire 2024 letter, original PDF pages 5-18
citations.quote:
I first heard of Forest River – the Indiana company Pete founded and managed – on
June 21, 2005. On that day I received a letter from an intermediary detailing relevant data about
the company, a recreational vehicle (“RV”) manufacturer. The writer said that Pete, the 100%
owner of Forest River, specifically wanted to sell to Berkshire.

citations.title: Berkshire 2024 letter, original PDF pages 5-18
citations.quote:
Let me pause to tell you the remarkable story of Pete Liegl, a man unknown to most
Berkshire shareholders but one who contributed many billions to their aggregate wealth. Pete
died in November, still working at 80.

citations.title: Berkshire 2024 letter, original PDF pages 5-18
citations.quote:
When we met, Pete
assured me that he wanted to keep running the business but would feel more comfortable if he
could assure financial security for his family.

citations.title: Berkshire 2024 letter, original PDF pages 5-18
citations.quote:
Then he surprised us: “Well, I
looked at Berkshire’s proxy statement and I wouldn’t want to make more than my boss, so pay
me $100,000 per year.” After I picked myself off the floor, Pete added: “But we will earn X (he
named a number) this year, and I would like an annual bonus of 10% of any earnings above what
the company is now delivering.” I replied: “OK Pete, but if Forest River makes any significant
acquisitions we will make an appropriate adjustment for the additional capital thus employed.”
